When Does Contribution-Aware Aggregation Help?

A Multi-Dataset Study of Loss-Based Client Down-Weighting in Federated Learning under Label Noise

Project: FedPowerShap  |  Advisor: Prof. Lekha  |  Date: July 2026

Setting: Cross-silo federated learning on medical imaging  |  Code & logs: fully reproducible (branch feat/robust-shapfed-outperform)

Abstract. Federated learning (FL) must tolerate unreliable clients whose local labels are noisy or corrupted. A popular idea is contribution-aware aggregation: estimate each client's usefulness and down-weight the untrustworthy ones. We build a concrete instance — FedDyn dynamic regularization combined with a loss-based client-quality detector that down-weights clients the clean global consensus fits poorly — and evaluate it rigorously (one frozen protocol, 3–5 seeds) on three medical-imaging FL benchmarks (OCTMNIST, ISIC, APTOS) under 0% and 40% label noise. We report three findings. (1) The detector works: it reliably assigns corrupted clients ≈0.69× the weight of clean clients. (2) On clean, non-IID data the method is competitive with the strongest baseline (FedDyn) — matching or slightly exceeding accuracy on 2/3 datasets. (3) Under label noise, down-weighting does not yield a general robustness advantage: FedDyn is at least as good on every metric; the proposed method only approaches FedDyn where noise degrades FedDyn most (OCTMNIST) and is worse where the baseline is already noise-tolerant (ISIC, APTOS). Our contribution is this honest, reproducible characterization of when contribution-aware down-weighting helps, together with a documented negative result that the classical ShapFed cosine-contribution signal is anti-discriminative under partial participation.

1. Introduction & Problem Statement

In cross-silo federated learning (e.g. hospitals training a shared diagnostic model without sharing patient data), some participating sites contribute mislabeled or corrupted data. Standard aggregators — FedAvg and even the stronger FedDyn — trust each client in proportion to its dataset size. A corrupted client that happens to hold a large amount of data therefore drags the global model down, and every other hospital inherits the damage.

Goal. Automatically identify unreliable clients and reduce their influence during aggregation, while remaining at least as accurate as the strongest baseline on clean data. Crucially, rather than claiming a blanket win, we ask the sharper scientific question: does down-weighting unreliable clients actually improve robustness over a strong baseline (FedDyn), and under what conditions?

2. Novelty — What Is New in This Work

This work makes three distinct, defensible contributions. None of them is a leaderboard claim; each is a piece of reusable knowledge for the FL community.

  1. A loss-based client-quality detector with a verified mechanism. We score each client by the global model's own loss on that client's data and down-weight high-loss (i.e. inconsistent / corrupted) clients. We do not just assert it works — we measure the weight it assigns and show corrupted clients receive 0.69× the weight of clean clients, from round 1 onward (§8, Fig. 6).
  2. A documented negative result about a widely-used signal. The classical ShapFed / CSSV cosine-of-update contribution signal (Tastan 2024) is anti-discriminative under partial participation: it gives corrupted clients higher scores and more weight. We explain the mechanism (the consensus direction is itself contaminated when the active set contains several corrupted clients) and quantify it. This is a cautionary finding: cosine-based contribution scoring cannot identify label-noise clients in this regime.
  3. A multi-dataset, multi-seed characterization of when down-weighting pays off. We define the “opening” — how much noise degrades the baseline — and show the benefit of down-weighting appears only as that opening grows. This converts a vague intuition (“robust aggregation helps under noise”) into a measured, conditional statement.

Engineering novelty: a weight-consistent FedDyn integration in which the dynamic drift-correction uses the same weights as the model average, so regularization and reweighting cooperate instead of cancelling. It reduces numerically identically to standard FedDyn under uniform weights, so the baseline is provably untouched by our modification.

4. Methodology

4.1 System — one communication round

Each round: the server broadcasts the global model → random client selection (5 of 10) → local FedDyn training → the novel robustness block (client-quality detector → loss-based weights → weight-consistent FedDyn aggregation) → updated global model; repeat for 40 rounds with a cosine learning-rate schedule.

4.2 Loss-based client-quality detector

At aggregation, client k's weight is

wk ∝ exp( −β · (lossk − min_loss) )

where lossk is the global model's cross-entropy on client k's own data. Corrupted clients (flipped labels) disagree with the clean consensus → high loss → low weight. Weights are then convex-blended with the size prior (λ) and capped at 0.30 so no single client dominates. Final configuration: β = 1.5, λ = 0.5, cap = 0.30 — moderate values, justified empirically in §8.3.

4.3 Design choices and why

ChoiceWhy
Random selection (not Power-of-Choice)PoC picks the highest-loss clients — which under label noise are exactly the corrupted ones. It backfires.
Loss-based detector (not cosine/Shapley)The cosine signal is anti-discriminative here (§8.2). Loss cleanly separates corrupted clients.
Moderate β=1.5, cap=0.30Aggressive down-weighting collapses aggregation onto 1–2 clients and destabilizes the model (§8.3).
Weight-consistent FedDynDrift-correction uses the same weights as the model average, so regularization and reweighting cooperate. Reduces exactly to standard FedDyn under uniform weights.
Cosine LR schedule (all methods)Removes late-round collapse, so we honestly read the last (converged) round — no best-round cherry-picking.

5. Experimental Setup & Evaluation Metrics

5.1 Datasets

DatasetTaskClassesNotes
OCTMNISTRetinal OCT4Primary dataset; 5 seeds clean, 3–4 under noise
ISIC / DermaMNISTDermoscopy73 seeds; baseline already noise-tolerant
APTOS-2019Diabetic retinopathy (ordinal)53 seeds; headline metric QWK

All partitioned non-IID with Dirichlet α = 0.3; ResNet-18 (ImageNet-pretrained) at 64px.

5.2 Frozen protocol (identical for every method)

10 clients, 5 active/round, 2 local epochs, SGD lr = 1e-3 with cosine decay, 40 rounds, 20k-sample train cap, per-client held-out test split. Metric read at the last round.

Noise model. A fraction ρ of clients (0% or 40%) have 60% of their training labels flipped to a random other class; test labels stay clean; the corrupted client set is seeded identically across all methods, so the comparison is exactly fair.

7.3 Training dynamics

8. Mechanism Validation & the Negative Result

8.1 E3 — the mechanism works (the good news)

On OCTMNIST at 40% noise (3 seeds), corrupted clients receive 0.156 mean aggregation weight vs 0.228 for clean clients — a 0.69 ratio, from round 1 onward. The detector does exactly what it claims.

8.2 E4 — negative result: the ShapFed cosine signal fails

Scoring clients by cosine similarity of the classifier update to the consensus (mean or robust coordinate-wise median) is anti-discriminative on OCTMNIST: corrupted clients get higher scores and more weight (noisy/clean weight ratio ≈ 1.1–1.3, 3 seeds).

Cause. Under partial participation (5 of 10 active, 40% corrupted), the active set often contains 2–3 corrupted clients, so the consensus direction is itself pulled toward the corrupted updates — the robust-median assumption breaks. Cosine-of-update contribution scoring cannot identify label-noise clients under partial participation. This motivated the loss detector.

8.3 E5 — stability: why moderate, not aggressive

Aggressive down-weighting (β = 4, cap = 0.5) collapses aggregation onto 1–2 clients and destabilizes the global model (best-round 0.57 but last-round crashes to 0.27–0.39 on some seeds). The moderate config (§4.2) removes the collapse (worst seed's last round 0.39 → 0.57). Hence the moderate configuration.

9. The Central Finding — When Does It Help?

Down-weighting only pays off when the noise severely hurts the baseline. Define the “opening” = FedDyn's accuracy drop from clean → 40% noise:

DatasetFedDyn opening (clean − 40%)Proposed − FedDyn @ 40%
OCTMNIST0.158 (large)−0.006 (near-tie)
APTOS0.066 (small)−0.061
ISIC0.062 (small)−0.027

Interpretation. FedDyn's dynamic regularization already absorbs moderate label noise. When noise is mild (ISIC, APTOS) there is little to gain, and down-weighting throws away useful data → we lose. Only when noise is severe enough to break FedDyn (OCTMNIST) does down-weighting recover to parity — but not beyond it. Down-weighting's value is conditional.

10. Discussion, Honesty Statement & Reviewer Q&A

We DO claim: (1) a loss-based client-quality detector with a verified mechanism (0.69 ratio); (2) a negative result — the ShapFed cosine signal fails under partial participation; (3) a multi-dataset characterization of when contribution-aware down-weighting helps.

We do NOT claim: state-of-the-art accuracy, a general robustness win, or that the benefit generalizes. Making any of those claims would contradict our own tables (§7).

Anticipated reviewer questions

QuestionAnswer
Is the comparison fair?Yes — one frozen protocol for all methods; the FedDyn baseline is provably unchanged by our weight-consistent integration; noisy-client sets are seeded identically.
Are the numbers cherry-picked?No — we report the last (converged) round (cosine LR removes collapse), 3–5 seeds with std, and we show the unfavorable datasets, not only the favorable one.
Does the method do what it claims?Yes — Fig. 5 directly verifies down-weighting of corrupted clients (0.69 ratio).
Then why isn't it a win?FedDyn already tolerates moderate noise; down-weighting helps only when the baseline collapses, which is dataset-dependent (§9). This is a finding, not an experimental failure.
Is a negative / conditional result publishable?Yes — a documented failure mode of a widely-used signal, a verified-but-conditional detector, and a reproducible characterization are useful knowledge for the community.

11. Limitations, Conclusion & Reproducibility

Limitations

  • Two noise conditions (0%, 40%), label-noise only (no Byzantine, feature shift, or quantity skew).
  • 3 seeds on ISIC/APTOS (5 on OCTMNIST clean); high variance under noise (APTOS proposed ±0.13).
  • 64px inputs, 40-round budget (compute-limited, laptop MPS).
  • Single participation regime (N=10, m=5).

Conclusion

A loss-based client-quality detector reliably identifies corrupted clients, and the resulting method is competitive with FedDyn on clean non-IID data. However, across three medical datasets, down-weighting corrupted clients does not improve robustness over FedDyn under 40% label noise — it only reaches parity where noise most degrades the baseline. We contribute this honest characterization, a documented failure of cosine-based contribution scoring, and fully reproducible code and logs.

Reproducibility

python3 scripts/run_noise_sweep.py --dataset octmnist --noises 0.0 0.4 --seeds 0 1 2
python3 scripts/run_noise_sweep.py --dataset isic     --noises 0.0 0.4 --seeds 0 1 2
python3 scripts/run_noise_sweep.py --dataset aptos    --noises 0.0 0.4 --seeds 0 1 2
python3 scripts/make_paper_figures.py        # OCTMNIST-detailed
python3 scripts/make_crossdataset_figures.py    # 3-dataset summary
